messages.subject: occuRN
messages.body_plain:
I'm interested in estimating abundance and detectability of plants
from repeat surveys. It seems to me that the Royle-Nichols 2003 model
(occuRN) might be just what I’m looking for.
As I’m a beginner to this, I’ve been trying to replicate the results
of Royle-Nichols on the example woodthrush and catbird data that comes
with the unmarked package. Unfortunately, the usage example in the R
documentation is very brief and the results I get are not the same as
those published.
Could anyone help me get over this hurdle I’ve come up against? A more
complete example of the use of occuRN might be all I need.
Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: RE: [SPAM] [unmarked] occuRN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Quentin,

you could use either the standard occupancy model (function occu()) or the Royle-Nichols occupancy model with abundance-induced detection heterogeneity for your modeling. The latter is probably somewhat more appropriate, because it should take account of the fact that plant abundance will vary from site to site and of the heterogeneity in p induced by this. On the other hand, using the standard model in my opinion should also be OK, even if overall, psi will be underestimated to the degree that there is detection heterogeneity. See the paper by Dorazio in Ecology (2007) for that.

Perhaps you could start some modeling with the occu() function to get acquainted with unmarked and then try out occuRN(). occu() has more documentation currently. If you want, I could send you a document  that gives more examples of the use of occu().

Regards  --  Marc

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] occuRN
messages.body_plain:
hi Quentin,

I'll send you a documentation about non-RN occupancy models for WinBUGS, which I recently wrote for a workshop. In it, I give several extended examples for how to use occu() for fitting the model to simulated and real data.

In my former life I was a plant ecologist, though now I work mostly with animals. In terms of occupancy, I don't see any difference between the analysis of plant and animal populations (there may be some differences when dealing with abundance; essentially, they have to do with the more ambiguous definition of the individual in plants). Actually, with some colleagues, we are currently using the classic occupancy model to investigate determinants of detection probability of 100 Swiss plant species at the scale of 1 km2. We are using data from a big Swiss biodiversity monitoting program, where a 2.5 km transect in each of 450 sites is walked twice per season. Almost no species has p=1 and on average over the 100 species, the per-survey p is 0.8.

You say that you want to do the same analysis for many species. In that case, the best framework for you would actually be multispecies site-occupancy models, which are (currently ?) not implemented in unmarked and you would have to use WinBUGS for that. Those models are described, for instance, in Dorazio et al. (Ecology, 2006), Kery and Royle (JAPPL, 2008), Zipkin et al. (around 2009-2011) and Yamaura et al. (JAPPL 2011). The last one may particularly interest you, since it is a multi-species RN-site occupancy model.

Kind regards --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks; those references will keep me busy. Yamaura et al. (2011)
does look useful, though it might be beyond my skill level with
Winbugs.
Your average plant detectability seems similar to what I've
experienced, though it's those plants with a much lower detectability
that interest me. After all, if you survey two or three times and your
detectability per survey is 0.8 then you will find most species and if
you don't find them you can assume they are very rare in the survey
area.
I admire the methodical Swiss. I work with UK data and although we
have an enormous quantity of data it is collected rather haphazardly.
This makes it very difficult to tackle statistically. Practically, all
assumptions of independence and random sampling are impossible to
make. The general approach is to avoid statistics by sampling
everywhere, but of course these leads to big disparities in recorder
effort.

Regards
Quentin

Hi Marc,

parboot does allow for covariates. However, if there are missing covariate values, the fit-statistic needs to be written so that they are ignored. It looks like the function we put in the vignette needs to be modified. It should work if you change the last line to:

sum((y-fv)^2/(fv*(1-fv)), na.rm=TRUE)

Regarding your second question, I think the high P-value is just due to chance. I simulated a new dataset and got a P-value close to the expected value of  0.5:

> m1

Call:
colext(psiformula = ~1, gammaformula = ~year - 1, epsilonformula = ~year -
    1, pformula = ~year - 1, data = simUMF, se=FALSE)

>  pb.gof

Call: parboot(object = m1, statistic = chisq, nsim = 50, report = 1)

Parametric Bootstrap Statistics:
    t0 mean(t0 - t_B) StdDev(t0 - t_B) Pr(t_B > t0)

1 7500          0.329             2.64        0.529

t_B quantiles:
      0% 2.5%  25%  50%  75% 97.5% 100%

t*1 7482 7499 7500 7500 7500  7500 7503

t0 = Original statistic compuated from data
t_B = Vector of bootstrap samples

I hacked the function "occu" this morning to allow for "false positive" errors. This version does NOT allow for covariates on false positive detection probability, but rather just handles a single "constant" value of false positive detection probability.

An ANCOVA includes an effect for each species level and a single coefficient for dpn, something like this:

occu(~esp ~ -1 +  esp + dpn, occe500)

You didn't really say, but I have a feeling that you actually want both an intercept and dpn covariate slope for each species:

occu(~esp ~ -1 + esp * dpn, occe500)

Note that I omitted the intercept for both models just to parameterize in terms of a separate intercept per species.

Hope that helps,
Ian

Hi Manuel,

Your code below is correct if you are trying to get predicted values of p for each site at _unique_ values of season. If you are trying to get predictions for each site _averaged_ over the levels of season, then you need to follow Ian and Andy's previous advice. This can be done using either linearComb or predict. If you want to use predict, then  you need to specify custom contrasts. These should be equivalent:

# Predictions of p for each site averaged over seasons
newData  <-  data.frame(site = factor(c("a", "b", "c")),
                        season = factor(c("a", "b", "c")))
contrasts(newData$season) <- matrix(1/3, 3, 2) # define custom contrasts

predict(mod2brid, type="det", newdata=newData, appendData=TRUE)

# Same thing using linearComb
backTransform(linearComb(mod2brid["det"],
    matrix(c(1,0,0,1/3,1/3,
             1,1,0,1/3,1/3,
             1,0,1,1/3,1/3), nrow=3, byrow=TRUE)))

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

   I would like to use the occu function in unmarked to calculate the sensitivities of PCR probes for detecting blood parasites based on repeated PCR amplification attempts from all of the blood samples (straightforward in the general case), but with the added twist of knowing a priori the infection status of birds.  I understand that it is not possible currently to fix parameter values for psi (or p), but it appears that there is another way for me to do what I want using occu, using the knownOcc option.  My question is: how exactly do I use knownOcc?

   The only documentation on this option that I have found anywhere is in the base R document that states that knownOcc works by providing occu with a “vector of sites that are known to be occupied.”  I can think of at least two ways in which to interpret this statement:

(1)    The “vector of sites” is a Boolean of the same length as the number of rows in the table of detection/non-detection data, in which a “1” at location i in the vector would indicate that the ith detection record was from an instance in which occupancy was known.

(2)    The “vector of sites” is a vector containing site identification information, such as row numbers or possibly a unique ID variable that needs to be added by the analyst, for only those sites at which occupancy is known.  This vector would be of variable length relative to the number of rows in the detection data, because the vector would only contain values for the records where true presence is known.

There are probably other ways of implementing the same functionality, as well.  Regardless, the sentence that I quoted above is the only documentation for knownOcc that I have been able to find.  I would be most grateful if someone could point me to more detailed documentation, or otherwise explain how knownOcc works.

   Thanks in advance!

Wesley

Hi Wesley,

I agree, that is somewhat confusing. knownOcc should be a vector of the "site numbers" for which occupancy is known a priori. So if you know that sites 3 and 7 were occupied (ie, rows 3 and 7 of y), then you would use knownOcc=c(3,7).

One quick comment. If you are only interested in the probability of detecting parasites given that parasites are known to be present (Pr(y_ij=1|z_i=1), you could use logistic regression on the subset of birds that are known to have parasites:

glm(cbind(detected, notDetected) ~ someCovariate, family=binomial, data=subsetOfBirdsWithParasites).

where "detected" is a column in the data indicating the number of detections made in N trials on bird i. "notDetected" would be another column in the data equal to N-detected.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tyler,

the N-mixture model fitted with pcount is the natural counterpart to the site-occupancy model when you have counts with imperfect detection, instead of detection/nondetection observations with imperfect detection. Counts contain more information about the underlying abundance distribution than detection/nondetection observations, therefore it's best not to throw away info by reducing them to detection/nondetections (a.k.a. "presence/absence" data).

Kind regards  --  Marc
